subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Burn surface area, classification, and inhalation injury
vignette: A 34-year-old sustains thermal burns covering the entire left arm and the entire anterior trunk, with no other areas involved.
question: Using the rule of 9s, what is the estimated percentage of total body surface area burned?
explanation_correct: The rule of 9s assigns 9% to each arm, 18% to each leg, 9% to the head, 18% to the anterior trunk, 18% to the posterior trunk, and 1% to the perineum. An entire arm is 9% and the anterior trunk is 18%, for a total of 27%. This estimate guides fluid resuscitation and assessment of burn severity.

explanation_incorrect.A: 18% would account for only the anterior trunk or one leg, omitting the arm.
explanation_incorrect.C: 36% would be the anterior and posterior trunk combined, not arm plus anterior trunk.
explanation_incorrect.D: 45% would overestimate; it would require additional burn areas not described.
explanation_incorrect.E: 9% accounts for only the arm and ignores the anterior trunk burn.

educationalObjective: Using the rule of 9s, an entire arm (9%) plus the anterior trunk (18%) equals 27% TBSA.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Burn surface area, classification, and inhalation injury
vignette: A patient is extracted from a burning building with facial burns, singed nasal hairs, and soot in the oropharynx. Bronchoscopy shows severe bronchial edema, congestion, and soot deposition.
question: Which of the following best describes the expected consequence of this inhalation injury?

options.text: Injury is confined to the upper airway because heat is completely filtered by the nose
Only particulates larger than 1 micrometer in diameter reach the distal airways
The damage is caused by an IgG-mediated autoimmune reaction in the bronchi
Heat, particulates, and irritants can cause chemical tracheobronchitis, edema, pneumonia, and ARDS
Bronchoscopy is typically normal despite severe symptoms

explanation_correct: Inhalation injury results from breathing noxious stimuli such as smoke. Heat, small particulates (less than 1 micrometer in diameter), and irritants such as ammonia cause chemical tracheobronchitis, edema, pneumonia, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Singed nasal hairs and soot in the oropharynx are common examination clues, and bronchoscopy shows severe edema, congestion, and soot deposition. This is a serious complication of burn injuries.

explanation_incorrect.A: Inhalation injury is not confined to the upper airway; distal airways and alveoli can be injured by small particulates and irritants.
explanation_incorrect.B: It is particulates smaller than 1 micrometer, not larger, that reach distal airways and cause injury.
explanation_incorrect.C: The injury is chemical and thermal, not an IgG-mediated autoimmune process.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bronchoscopy typically shows marked edema, congestion, and soot, not normal findings.

educationalObjective: Inhalation injury from smoke heat, fine particulates, and irritants causes chemical tracheobronchitis, edema, pneumonia, and ARDS; singed nasal hairs and soot are key signs.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Burn surface area, classification, and inhalation injury
vignette: A patient has a burn wound with blisters, swelling, and warmth. The area blanches with pressure and is exquisitely painful to temperature changes and air exposure.
question: Which burn classification is most consistent with these findings?

options.text: Superficial partial-thickness burn involving epidermis and papillary dermis
Superficial burn involving epidermis only
Deep partial-thickness burn involving epidermis and reticular dermis
Full-thickness burn involving epidermis and entire dermis
Deeper injury burn involving fascia and muscle

explanation_correct: A superficial partial-thickness burn involves the epidermis and papillary dermis. It produces blisters, blanches with pressure, and is swollen and warm, with pain to temperature and air exposure. This distinguishes it from a superficial burn, which is epidermis only with dry blanching redness and no blisters, and from deeper burns that do not blanch and are less painful.

explanation_incorrect.B: A superficial burn involves only epidermis, appears as dry blanching redness without blisters, and is not described as blistered and swollen.
explanation_incorrect.C: A deep partial-thickness burn extends into the reticular dermis, does not blanch, and is painless except to pressure.
explanation_incorrect.D: A full-thickness burn is white, waxy, dry, and leathery, does not blanch, and is painless except to deep pressure.
explanation_incorrect.E: A deeper injury burn involves fascia and muscle and is painless, not a blanching blistered wound.

educationalObjective: Blisters, blanching, swelling, warmth, and pain to air/temperature define a superficial partial-thickness burn (epidermis and papillary dermis).

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Burn surface area, classification, and inhalation injury
vignette: A burn wound is white, waxy, dry, inelastic, and leathery. It does not blanch with pressure, has no blisters, and is painless except when deep pressure is applied.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this burn?

options.text: Superficial burn, involving epidermis only, with dry blanching redness and pain
Superficial partial-thickness burn, with blisters that blanch and pain to air
Deep partial-thickness burn, with easily unroofed blisters, no blanching, and perception of pressure only
Deeper injury burn, with involvement of fascia and muscle
Full-thickness burn, involving epidermis and entire dermis, white and leathery, no blanching, painless except to deep pressure

explanation_correct: A full-thickness burn destroys the epidermis and the entire dermis. The wound appears white, waxy, dry, inelastic, and leathery, does not blanch with pressure, and is painless except for deep pressure because nerve endings are destroyed. It lacks blisters, and healing typically requires grafting. These features distinguish it from a deep partial-thickness burn, which has easily unroofed blisters and retains pressure sensation.

explanation_incorrect.A: A superficial burn is painful, blanches, and has no leathery texture or deep-pressure-only sensation.
explanation_incorrect.B: A superficial partial-thickness burn blanches and is painful to temperature and air, unlike this painless non-blanching wound.
explanation_incorrect.C: A deep partial-thickness burn has blisters that are easily unroofed, does not blanch, and retains pressure perception, but it is not white, waxy, and leathery like this wound.
explanation_incorrect.D: A deeper injury burn involves fascia and muscle; the description here is confined to skin with classic full-thickness features.

educationalObjective: A white, waxy, dry, leathery, non-blanching wound that is painless except to deep pressure is a full-thickness burn.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Burn surface area, classification, and inhalation injury
vignette: A burn extends through the epidermis and dermis with visible involvement of the underlying fascia and muscle. The wound is white, dry, and inelastic and does not blanch.
question: Which term best describes this burn depth?

options.text: Superficial burn
Superficial partial-thickness burn
Deeper injury burn
Deep partial-thickness burn
Full-thickness burn

explanation_correct: A deeper injury burn extends beyond the epidermis and dermis to involve underlying tissues such as fascia and muscle. The wound is white, dry, and inelastic and does not blanch, and it is painless with at most some perception of deep pressure. The defining feature here is involvement of fascia and muscle, which distinguishes it from a full-thickness burn that is limited to the epidermis and full-thickness dermis.

explanation_incorrect.A: A superficial burn is confined to the epidermis and is painful, red, and blanching.
explanation_incorrect.B: A superficial partial-thickness burn involves the papillary dermis, blanches, and is painful.
explanation_incorrect.D: A deep partial-thickness burn involves the reticular dermis but not fascia or muscle.
explanation_incorrect.E: A full-thickness burn involves the epidermis and entire dermis but not the underlying fascia and muscle.

educationalObjective: Burns extending into fascia or muscle are classified as deeper injury burns, beyond full-thickness skin involvement.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Burn surface area, classification, and inhalation injury
vignette: A medical student is reviewing the rule of 9s for burn surface area estimation.
question: Which of the following correctly pairs the body surface area assigned to the perineum and to the entire head?

options.text: Perineum 9%, entire head 18%
Perineum 1%, entire head 9%
Perineum 1%, entire head 18%
Perineum 5%, entire head 9%
Perineum 9%, entire head 9%

explanation_correct: In the rule of 9s, the perineum is assigned 1% of total body surface area and the entire head is assigned 9%. Each arm is 9%, each leg is 18%, and the anterior and posterior trunk are each 18%, summing to 100%. These values allow rapid estimation of burn extent for resuscitation decisions.

explanation_incorrect.A: The perineum is 1%, not 9%, and the head is 9%, not 18%.
explanation_incorrect.C: The head is 9%, not 18%; 18% corresponds to an entire leg or half the trunk.
explanation_incorrect.E: The perineum is 1%, not 9%, although the head value of 9% is correct.

educationalObjective: In the rule of 9s the perineum is 1% and the entire head is 9% of total body surface area.
